metadata.title: On weight initialization in deep neural networks

extraction_notes.note: The informal proof of Proposition 1 ends with \qedsymbol and no period, so the finishing step flags it as ending mid-sentence; the span is the author's full argument.

Label eq:tanh1 is defined twice (for v ~ 1/sqrt(N) and for the tanh pdf); the figure caption's \ref to it means the pdf (EP16). Also \enum{seq1} sits outside its equation, so eq:seq1 attaches to a section heading.
The text says the 30-layer network converges and the 22-layer one does not, which reverses the earlier description; the statement is copied as written.
Definition or claim: the sentence asserts equal moments by symmetry, but its main role is introducing $\mu_m$ and $s_m^2$.
The main results (general initialization formula, re-derived He initialization) are numbered equations that the text never names as results, so they stay equation nodes.
Single sentences introduce several symbols at once; a sentence can't be split, so each is one definition node with all symbols in definiendum.

Most of the argument is a chain of prose derivations linking numbered equations, with no proof environments. The equation-to-equation dependencies were added as uses edges by hand, and the connecting prose gets no node.
The CIFAR-10 experimental protocol (architecture, 10 training iterations, top-5 accuracy) is not an algorithm node; only its reported outcome is kept as a numerical claim.

nodes.statement: Using the recursions in () and (), x_m(k) can be expressed as some non-linear function of the weights in the first m-1 layers, and the inputs to the first layer. Since the weights in the m^th layer are independent of the inputs to the first layer and the weights in all other layers, the weights in the m^th layer will also be independent of any non-linear function of these quantities. Therefore, W_m(i,j) is independent of x_m(k) for all values of i, j and k. Furthermore, since W_m(i,j) is independent of x_m(k) and x_m(l), W_m(i,j) will also be independent of x_m(k)x_m(l) linebreak Taking expectations in () and using proposition 1, along with the fact that E(bfW_m(i,j)) = 0 yields r_m = E(y_m(i)) = sumlimits_j=1^j=N E(bfW_m(i,j))E(x_m(j)) = 0. enumin201 Therefore, u_m^2 = Var(y_m(i)) = Eleft(y_m(i)^2right) - left(E(y_m(i))right)^2 = Eleft(y_m(i)^2right). Using (), u_m^2 &= Eleft(sumlimits_j=1^j=NbfW_m(i,j)x_m(j)right)^2 \\ &= sumlimits_j=1^j=N Eleft(bfW_m(i,j)^2x_m(j)^2right) + 2sum Eleft(bfW_m(i,j)x_m(j)bfW_m(k,l)x_m(l)right). \\ enumin203 From proposition 1, bfW_m(i,j) and bfW_m(k,l) will (a) be independent of each other, and (b) be independent of x_m(j)x_m(l). Using these results, along with the fact that E(bfW_m(i,j)) = 0 gives Eleft(bfW_m(i,j)x_m(j)bfW_m(k,l)x_m(l)right) = E(bfW_m(i,j))E(bfW_m(k,l))E(x_m(j)x_m(l)) = 0. enumin2041 Plugging () into () gives u_m^2 &= sumlimits_j=1^j=N Eleft(bfW_m(i,j)^2x_m(j)^2right) \\ &= sumlimits_j=1^j=N Eleft(bfW_m(i,j)^2right)Eleft(x_m(j)^2right) \\ &= Nv^2(s_m^2 + mu_m^2) \\ enumin204 for all i.

nodes.statement: For the first iteration, note that E(p_ij) = Eleft(bfW_m(i,j)x_m(j)right) = Eleft(bfW_m(i,j)right)Eleft(x_m(j)right) = 0. Furthermore, for j neq k, Cov(p_ij,p_ik)&= E(p_ijp_ik) - E(p_ij)E(p_ik) \\ &= E(p_ijp_ik) \\ &= Eleft(bfW_m(i,j)x_m(j)bfW_m(i,k)x_m(k)right) = 0,\\ where the last equality follows from (). This implies that p_i1, p_i2 ... p_iN are independent and identically distributed random variables. Therefore by the Central Limit Theorem, we expect y_m(i) = sumlimits_j=1^j=N p_ij to converge to a normal distribution when N is large . Even when p_i1, p_i2 ... p_iN are dependent and not identically distributed, the conditions required to ensure that y_m(i) = sumlimits_j=1^j=N p_ij converges to a normal distribution are weak (for a list of all the conditions, see Theorem 2.8.2 in ). Thus, y_m(i) is expected to to be approximately normally distributed during most iterations. linebreak The analysis thus far has focused on providing general insights into the distribution of y_m(i) resulting from equation (). In order to analyze the role of the non-linearity induced by (), assumptions need to be made about the nature of g(x).
nodes.raw_latex:
\noindent
\noindent
For the first iteration, note that $E(p_{ij}) = E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j)\right) = E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)\right)E\left(x_{m}(j)\right)  = 0$. Furthermore, for $j \neq k$,
\begin{equation} 
\begin{split}
Cov(p_{ij},p_{ik})&= E(p_{ij}p_{ik}) - E(p_{ij})E(p_{ik}) \\
&=  E(p_{ij}p_{ik}) \\
&= E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j){\bf{W}}_{m}(i,k)x_{m}(k)\right) = 0,\\ 
\end{split}
\end{equation}
where the last equality follows from (\ref {eq:in2041}). This implies that $p_{i1}$, $p_{i2}$ ... $p_{iN}$ are independent and identically distributed random variables. Therefore by the Central Limit Theorem, we expect $y_{m}(i) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} p_{ij}$ to converge to a normal distribution when $N$ is large \cite{lehmann2004elements}.
Even when $p_{i1}$, $p_{i2}$ ... $p_{iN}$ are dependent and not identically distributed, the conditions required to ensure that  $y_{m}(i) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} p_{ij}$ converges to a normal distribution are weak (for a list of all the conditions, see Theorem 2.8.2 in \cite{lehmann2004elements}). Thus,  $y_{m}(i)$ is expected to  to be approximately normally distributed  during most iterations.
\qedsymbol 
\linebreak
\newline

Therefore, from () and (), with g(0) = 0 and g'(0) = 1, we have mu_m = 0 and s_m+1^2 = frac13s_m^2 < s_m^2 enumseq1 respectively. From (), this implies that u_m+1^2<u_m^2 for all m (i.e., u_m^2 is a decreasing function of m). Furthermore from proposition 2, y_m(i) sim calN(0,u_m^2). Therefore, x_m+1(i) will be the tanh transformation of a normal random variable. Using results from , x_m+1(i) = mboxtanh(y_m(i)) will have a probability density function (pdf) given by f(y) = frac11-y^2frac1sqrt2pi u_m^2mboxe^left(-fract_y^22u_m^2right) enumtanh1, where t_y = frac12 lnleft(frac1+y1-yright). Plots of this pdf for different values of u_m (provided in Figure ) produce trends similar to those observed by the simulation studies of (figure 4 in their paper). A comparison of Figure and figure 4 of suggests that u_m^2 is a decreasing function of m, as is expected.
